name: Nopala Chatino
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wardle, Ed & Linda Wardle. 1975. Phonemics Statement - Nopala Chatino. 2nd draft, July 6, 1975 (consultant: Barbara Hollenbach, handwritten). Typescript, 9 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives, Mexico Branch (Bartholomew Collection of Unpublished Materials), entry 31009. | Wardle, Edward & Linda Wardle. 1980. Cuento 'ine' cha'tño: narraciones en chatino de Nopala, Oaxaca. Tlalocan 8: 251-256. doi:10.19130/iifl.tlalocan.1980.52 (UNAM, open access).
catalog_locator: Wardle & Wardle 1975: typescript p. 1, sec. I 'The Word', paragraphs 1-3 and the clitic paragraph at the foot of the page; p. 2, sec. II 'The Syllable'; p. 9, sec. IV 'Tone'. Wardle & Wardle 1980: p. 256, 'Aclaraciones sobre el Alfabeto', item 1.
catalog_quote: [Wardle & Wardle 1980: 256] 1. Las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba y no llevan acento escrito. Por ejemplo: jija tortilla / jica palo. [Wardle & Wardle 1975: 1, sec. I The Word] The word level in Chatino is where it all happens. [Stress] {typed word struck through}, phonemic tone, length, and nasalization are all features of the word level since they all occur only on the [final] {struck, handwritten word above, read as 'stressed'} syllable. Chatino words may be one or two syllables in length with the following exceptions: 1) some words like: /lakuso?/ 'turkey' /lakwi?ya/ 'hawk' will probably eventually prove to be seqquences of two morphemes. 2) and some Spanish loan words such as: /pelota?/ 'ball' are three syllables in length. Chatino speakers of all dialects "put all thier eggs in one basket" by the importance of the final syllable, and in the Nopala dialect that emphasis is so great that the rest of the word may be phonologically altered, or even dropped altogether in the speech of some individuals. This results in an uneven distribution of phonemes between stressed and unstressed syllables; fewer being found in the latter than in the former. It also results in severe limitations upon the syllable structure in the unstressed position.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Se usa aquí el alfabeto elaborado en el análisis preliminar del chatino de Nopala. [...] 1. Las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba y no llevan acento escrito. Por ejemplo: jija 'tortilla', jica 'palo'.
new_statements.translation: The alphabet used here is the one developed in the preliminary analysis of Nopala Chatino. [...] 1. Chatino words are pronounced with greater force on the last syllable and carry no written accent. For example: jija 'tortilla', jica 'stick'.
new_statements.citation: Wardle, Edward & Linda Wardle. 1980. Cuento 'ine' cha'tño: narraciones en chatino de Nopala, Oaxaca. Tlalocan 8: 251-256. doi:10.19130/iifl.tlalocan.1980.52 (UNAM, open access).
new_statements.locator: p. 256, 'Aclaraciones sobre el Alfabeto', item 1 (PDF page 6 of 6)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: is a 6-page OmniPage-scanned PDF (text present); extracted text of PDF page 6 (printed p. 256, header '256 TLALOCAN') gives the section 'Aclaraciones sobre el Alfabeto' with, verbatim: 'Se usa aquí el alfabeto elaborado en el análisis preliminar del chatino de Nopala. [..] 1. Las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba y no llevan acento escrito. Por ejemplo: jija tortilla / jica palo'. In the the preamble is at lines 181-182 and item 1 at lines 188-191 (the compiler 'line 188-191' covers the stress sentence itself). Reading: 'mayor fuerza en la última sílaba' with disyllabic examples = fixed: final syllable word stress; the section is an orthograph…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word (the examples jija, jica show that Nopala retains disyllabic words, so 'last syllable' is not vacuous). Corroborated for the Teotepec variety of the same ISO/Glottolog language by McIntosh 2015 p. 44: 'Syllable stress in Chatino occurs on the ultimate syllable (Upson and Longacre, 1965; Pride, 1997). In monosyllabic varieties of Chatino stress occurs on the syllable.' (repeated p. 217, sec. 6.2.1) — Teotepec words are monosyllabic, so stress sits on the sole (= final) syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Wardle & Wardle 1980: none. McIntosh 2015 p. 217 lists lexemes that violate the one-syllable phonological word (Spanish names /liF pa/ 'Felipa', /RiF ke/ 'Enrique', some compounds, 'a handful of rogue disyllables e.g. jakwa four') but does not say where stress falls in them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('las palabras chatinas'), stated as an orthographic note justifying the absence of a written accent; based on the authors' 'preliminary analysis' (their 1975 SIL 'Phonemics Statement', not obtained). McIntosh's statement is about the syllable/phonological word (= stem) and is itself a generalisation citing Upson & Longacre 1965 (comparative Chatino) and Pride 1997 (Panixtlahuaca), not a Teotepec-specific finding; the language is tonal (McIntosh: nine tones, fourteen tone sequences), and neither source discusses phonetic correlates of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Two first-hand statements, both inside Glottolog's nopa1235/cya (which has no dialect children): (1) Wardle & Wardle 1980 describe the Chatino of Santos Reyes Nopala itself (district of Juquila; consultants Antonio Quintas, Leoncio Quintas, Melchor Zarate) — the namesake variety; (2) McIntosh 2015 describes Santa Lucia Teotepec Eastern Chatino (agencia of the municipio Santos Reyes Nopala), which he labels ISO 639-3 cya and which Glottolog files under nopa1235 as its two descriptive refs. Caution: Glottolog's third 'med' and WALS's sole source for cht, McKaughan 1954 'Chatino formulas and phonemes', is a description of Yaitepec Eastern Chatino (a separate Glottolog language) per Sullivant 2015 p. 34; only McKaughan & McKaughan 1951 (vocabulary) is Nopala.

new_statements.quote: Stress, phonemic tone, length, and nasalization are all features of the word level since they all occur only on the final syllable. [...] Chatino speakers of all dialects "put all thier eggs in one basket" by the importance of the final syllable, and in the Nopala dialect that emphasis is so great that the rest of the word may be phonologically altered, or even dropped altogether in the speech of some individuals. [...] These clitics do not alter the normal phonology of the word, since stress tone, etc. remain just as they would be without the clitic. If one is unfamiliar with the clitic, however, it would appear that stress is falling on the penultimate syllable with a post-clitic.
new_statements.citation: Wardle, Ed & Linda Wardle. 1975. Phonemics Statement - Nopala Chatino. Typescript with handwritten corrections, 9 pp. Draft posted 'as is'. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 31009.
new_statements.locator: typescript p. 1 (p. 2), sec. I 'The Word'; also p. 9 (p. 10), sec. IV 'Tone'
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Read p. 2 (typescript p. 1) and p. 10 (p. 9) from page scan at 200 and 400 dpi. Typed text: 'The word level in Chatino is where it all happens. Stress, phonemic tone, length, and nasalization are all features of the word level since they all occur only on the final syllable.' -- verbatim, but 'Stress' and 'final' are struck through by hand, with 'stressed' written above 'final' (2nd draft, July 6, 1975; marginal 'Consultant: Barbara Hollenbach'). 'Chatino speakers of all dialects "put all thier eggs in one basket" by the importance of the final syllable, and in the Nopala dialect that emphasis is so great that the rest of the word may be phonologically altered, or even dropped altogether in…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final syllable) and as Wardle & Wardle 1980 p. 256; adds the clitic domain, the reduced unstressed inventory and devoicing, and the tone-on-stressed-syllable link. Nopala dialect proper.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word (words are one or two syllables, rarely three); stress, contrastive tone, length and nasalization are all confined to that final stressed syllable. Enclitics (na- negation, -no 1pl, -?a 1pl excl, -?o 'with') lie outside the stress domain, so a word plus post-clitic surfaces with apparent penultimate stress. Unstressed (non-final) syllables have a reduced phoneme inventory (only /i u/ among vowels, 13 consonants) and undergo regressive vowel devoicing. p. 9: 'Chatino tone is a feature of the word, and is contrastive only on the final syllable. Unstressed syllables carry a non-contrastive tone'.
new_statements.exceptions: Three-syllable words (/lakuso?/ 'turkey', /lakwi?ya/ 'hawk', expected to be two morphemes; Spanish loans such as /pelota?/ 'ball') are exceptions to the 1-2 syllable template, with no separate stress placement given. Post-clitics make stress look penultimate. On this 2nd draft the words 'Stress' and 'final' in the first sentence (and 'the final' on p. 9) carry handwritten strike-throughs with illegible substitutions, i.e. the authors were revising the wording (probably to 'stressed syllable'), not the placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Wardle & Wardle 1975 and Wardle 1976 describe the Nopala dialect proper (Santos Reyes Nopala), the same variety as the catalog's existing Wardle & Wardle 1980 quote; the 1975 statement contrasts it with a 'related dialect' (Yaitepec, via Pride and Upson) that shares 75% intelligibility but differs in basic word tones. McKaughan 1954 describes Yaitepec Chatino (district of Juquila), despite WALS filing it under 'Chatino (Nopala)' cht. Glottolog nopa1235 has no dialect children; its descriptive references (McIntosh 2011, 2015, already held by the project) are for Santa Lucia Teotepec.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'Tonos en aislamiento' (p. 3): 'El análisis de los tonos en el chatino de Teotepec indica la presencia de nueve tonos en aislamiento y un tono no marcado.' Tones written 0 (super alto) to 4 (bajo): level /1/ /2/ /3/; rising /31/ /21/ /20/; falling /13/ /23/ /34/; plus relaxed unmarked /r/ (Cuadro 1). Tone /1/ generates a floating tone in sandhi (/1+0/). Sec. 1.1: all roots monosyllabic, each bears a tone; TBU = syllable; template (N)(C)(C)CV(V nasal)(7). Sec. 3 sandhi processes, sec. 4 'Tonos fuertes y débiles', Appendices A-B cognate correspondences with other Eastern Chatino varietie…
